strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: existing SFT-oriented low-rank initialization schemes (PiSSA, MiLoRA) are not designed for RLVR's distinct update geometry, and the paper offers a plausible mechanistic story (principal vs. non-principal subspace updates) grounded in cited prior mechanistic analyses.

The proposed masking + SVD initialization (combining spectral low-curvature and Euclidean low-magnitude priors) is a reasonably novel synthesis that yields a dense, hardware-friendly parameterization, avoiding the unstructured-sparsity efficiency bottleneck of prior sparse fine-tuning approaches.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: two backbone families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), multiple ID math benchmarks and OOD benchmarks (code, science, general knowledge), plus efficiency measurements (params, time/it, VRAM) and training-dynamics/stability stress tests under aggressive learning rates.

The mechanism analysis (singular value spectrum, Normalized Spectral Shift, subspace alignment S(k)) provides some quantitative grounding for the geometric claims and helps explain why PiSSA collapses (high overlap with principal subspace) versus GeoRA's stability.
Clear writing and useful figures (architecture comparison, mask construction, training dynamics) that make the method easy to follow.
weaknesses: No reported variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds anywhere despite RLVR being a notoriously high-variance training regime; all comparisons in Tables 1–4 and Figures 3–5 appear to be single runs, undermining the statistical reliability of claims that GeoRA 'consistently outperforms' baselines, especially given several margins (e.g., 34.04 vs 33.77 Avg for Qwen3-8B FullFT) are small.

The central claim that a rank-16 PEFT method (0.04B trainable params) surpasses Full Fine-Tuning (8B params) on in-distribution math benchmarks is extraordinary and under-justified; no ablation isolates whether this stems from insufficient FullFT hyperparameter tuning, overfitting of the masking/init heuristic to the eval sets, or a genuine regularization effect, and no learning-rate/training-budget sweep is reported for FullFT as is done for GeoRA in Figure 4.

Core ablations (Table 3, initialization strategy and mask components) and part of the stability analysis (Figure 5) are conducted on a different, smaller model (Qwen3-4B) and a different, easier dataset (GSM8K) than the main results (Qwen3-8B/Llama-3.1-8B on DeepMath-103K), so the paper's central design choices are not directly validated in the primary experimental setting.

The construction of the spectral mask M_Spec depends on a rank-r SVD approximation Ŵ_r of the same weight matrix that GeoRA will later re-SVD to build W_Geo, creating a somewhat circular pipeline; the added value of this two-stage mask-then-SVD procedure over directly initializing from minor/near-zero components (as in MiLoRA, but with better amplitude scaling) is not clearly isolated by ablation.

The mechanism analysis in Section 5.2 (NSS, S_Head, S_Tail) largely reports properties that are close to guaranteed by construction (GeoRA's update lives in the masked low-magnitude subspace by design), so these numbers offer limited independent evidence of a causal geometric advantage rather than a restatement of the method's construction.

Baseline coverage omits several PEFT variants discussed in Related Work (AdaLoRA, DoRA, VeRA) that could also serve as competitive comparisons; only LoRA, PiSSA, MiLoRA, SparseFT, and FullFT are benchmarked.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: exact GRPO hyperparameters (batch size, number of rollouts, KL coefficient), evaluation protocol for AIME/MATH-500 (pass@1 vs. averaged over samples, number of samples), and whether baseline methods received independent hyperparameter tuning (rank, learning rate) beyond the shared sweep in Figure 4 are not specified, making exact replication difficult.

AIME24/25 scores (only 30 problems each) are reported to two decimal places without clarifying how these fractional values arise (e.g., averaging over multiple sampled generations), which is left unexplained and affects interpretability of the fine-grained differences highlighted as 'significant.'

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and well-motivated problem: adapting PEFT initialization strategies to the geometry of RLVR updates rather than naively reusing SFT-oriented spectral priors (PiSSA, MiLoRA).

The proposed masking mechanism (union of a spectral low-curvature prior and a Euclidean magnitude prior) followed by SVD-based initialization within this constrained subspace is a reasonably novel and intuitive way to combine the benefits of structured low-rank adapters with the empirical observation that effective RL updates are low-magnitude/off-principal.

The efficiency argument is compelling and clearly explained: by using dense low-rank operators instead of unstructured sparse masks, GeoRA avoids the GPU overhead that limits prior sparse fine-tuning approaches, and Table 2 shows a credible wall-clock/VRAM benefit.

The mechanism analysis (singular value spectra, NSS, subspace alignment S(k)) provides a plausible internal consistency story connecting the design choices to observed training stability, and the PiSSA KL-divergence collapse experiment (Figure 5) is a nice illustrative stress test.
weaknesses: No variance/seed reporting anywhere in the paper: all RL results (Table 1, Table 3, Figures 3-5) are presented as single point estimates despite GRPO/RLVR training being well known to have high run-to-run variance; many of the claimed 'wins' (e.g., GeoRA 34.04 vs FullFT 33.77 on Qwen3-8B, or 24.51 vs 24.37 on Llama) are well within plausible noise, undermining the central claim of consistent SOTA performance.

Inconsistent experimental protocol across sections: main results use Qwen3-8B-Base/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on DeepMath-103K, while all ablations (initialization strategy, mask components) switch to an entirely different model (Qwen3-4B-Base) and dataset (GSM8K) with no justification, making it impossible to verify whether the ablation conclusions transfer to the main setting where the headline numbers are reported.

Marginal and sometimes non-monotonic improvements (e.g., GeoRA underperforms FullFT on MATH500 for both backbones; AIME25 gain is only 0.42 pp on Qwen) are presented with inflated rhetoric ('significantly outperforming', 'strictly dominant trajectory', 'remarkable robustness') not warranted by the size of the effects.

Key hyperparameters (rank r=16, sparsity ratio ρ=0.2) appear to be fixed without a systematic ablation in the main text; the promised 'parameter sensitivity analysis... under ultra-low rank or high sparsity' is only described in prose with no accompanying table/figure, so robustness claims cannot be verified.

Reproducibility is weak: no code/data release is mentioned, and crucial implementation details (learning-rate schedules, number of GRPO rollouts, training steps, batch sizes, how the 'SparseFT (2MGeo masking)' baseline is actually implemented) are not specified, making the experiments difficult to replicate.

The mechanistic/theoretical claims (e.g., 'RLVR provably learns off the principals', specific geometric characterizations of RL updates) are largely imported from concurrent/contemporaneous arXiv preprints as established fact rather than independently validated in a controlled way within this paper; the causal narrative in Section 5 is correlational (spectrum shape, NSS, S(k) alignment) but presented as if it mechanistically explains performance differences.

Evaluation relies on small benchmarks with high variance (AIME has very few items per year), yet single-run accuracy differences of a few percentage points are treated as decisive evidence of superiority.

Baseline tuning is unclear—it's not stated whether PiSSA, MiLoRA, and LoRA were given comparable hyperparameter search budgets, raising concern that baseline underperformance (e.g., PiSSA's collapse) may partly reflect suboptimal tuning rather than an inherent geometric flaw.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: existing SFT-oriented low-rank adaptation initialization schemes (PiSSA, MiLoRA) are shown, both conceptually and empirically, to be mismatched with RLVR's optimization dynamics.

The proposed masking-then-SVD construction (spectral + Euclidean priors) is a reasonably novel and clearly described mechanism for identifying a stable, RLVR-compatible low-rank subspace while retaining dense-operator compatibility (avoiding the hardware inefficiency of unstructured sparse fine-tuning).

The mechanism analysis (Section 5), including singular-value spectrum comparisons, Normalized Spectral Shift, and Head/Tail subspace alignment, provides a coherent narrative connecting the method's design to its empirical stability advantages, and the KL-divergence/reward collapse case study (Fig. 5) is a compelling qualitative demonstration of the claimed instability mechanism in PiSSA.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental scope for a PEFT paper: two backbone families (Qwen, Llama), ID and OOD evaluation, efficiency comparisons, learning-rate sensitivity, and several ablations (initialization strategy, mask components).
weaknesses: No variance/seed information is reported anywhere in the paper; RLVR training is well known to be high-variance and prone to instability, yet all main results (Table 1), ablations (Table 3), and mechanism analyses (Table 4) appear to be single-run numbers, making it impossible to assess whether the (often small, e.g., 34.04 vs 33.77 FullFT, 0.27 pts) reported gains are statistically meaningful.

The main results are obtained on only one training dataset (DeepMath-103K) and one RL algorithm (GRPO); ablations are conducted on a different, smaller model (Qwen3-4B-Base) and a much easier dataset (GSM8K) than the main experiments, weakening the link between the ablation conclusions and the paper's headline claims.

The 'SparseFT' baseline appears to be an in-house construction (based on '2×M_Geo masking') rather than a reproduction of an actual published sparse-RL method (e.g., the cited Mukherjee et al. 2025 or Zhu et al. 2025), so the claimed efficiency/performance comparison against 'sparse fine-tuning approaches' in the introduction is not well substantiated by comparison to real prior sparse methods.

The paper claims GeoRA surpasses Full Fine-Tuning on math benchmarks and matches/exceeds it on OOD tasks; such a strong and somewhat counter-intuitive claim requires stronger evidence (e.g., confirmation that FullFT hyperparameters were adequately tuned, multiple seeds) to rule out under-tuning as an explanation.

Reproducibility is limited: key implementation details (learning rate schedules, batch sizes, GRPO hyperparameters, number of training steps, how rank r=16 and sparsity ρ=0.2 were selected, layer selection for masking) are not specified in the visible manuscript, and no code/data release is mentioned.

The extra SVD-then-mask-then-SVD pipeline (compute rank-r truncation to build the spectral mask, then a second SVD on the masked matrix) adds non-trivial preprocessing complexity and computational cost that is acknowledged only briefly in the Limitations section without quantification.

Claimed generality (parameter sensitivity to rank=4 and sparsity=10%) is asserted in text but no supporting numbers/figures for these 'extreme conditions' are shown in the paper, leaving this claim unverified.

Mechanism-analysis metrics (Table 4, Figure 6) are reported for a single layer (Layer 33 of Qwen3-8B) without clarifying whether trends generalize across layers, limiting the strength of the geometric claims as evidence for the overall method.

strengths: Addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: parameter-efficient adaptation methods specifically tailored to RLVR's distinct optimization geometry, as opposed to SFT-oriented spectral priors like PiSSA.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span multiple model families (Qwen, Llama), scales (1.5B to 32B), and RLVR domains (math, medicine, coding), with both ID and OOD evaluation to assess generalization/forgetting.

Reasonably thorough ablations (initialization strategy, individual mask components) and hyperparameter robustness studies (learning rate, rank, sparsity) that support the internal consistency of the design choices.

The mechanism analysis (singular value spectrum comparisons, Normalized Spectral Shift, subspace alignment) offers some interpretability into why GeoRA's updates might be more stable than PiSSA/MiLoRA/LoRA, and is a nice complement to the raw accuracy tables.

Efficiency comparison against SparseFT and FullFT plausibly demonstrates that GeoRA avoids the hardware inefficiency of unstructured sparse updates while retaining a small trainable parameter footprint.
weaknesses: All main results appear to be based on a single random run (explicitly stated in Appendix C.1: "a single random run"), with no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds reported. This is a significant soundness concern given RLVR/GRPO training is known to be high-variance, and many reported gains over baselines are small (often <1-2 points), making it hard to determine whether GeoRA's improvements are statistically meaningful or within run-to-run noise.

The results are not uniformly favorable to GeoRA: e.g., GPQA on Qwen3-8B is won by MiLoRA, IFEval score for GeoRA is below the pre-RLVR Base model (suggesting some forgetting despite the paper's claim of "less forgetting"), and HumanEval on the coding task is won by FullFT/other methods over GeoRA — these exceptions are not discussed or reconciled with the paper's general narrative.

The conceptual justification for the geometric prior (MSpec, MEuc) is somewhat heuristic and only loosely connected to the mechanistic analysis presented later: the masks are computed purely from the static pre-trained weight matrix W, whereas the supporting evidence for "RLVR favors a compressible, anisotropic subspace" is derived post hoc from the actual FullFT update ΔW. The paper does not establish a rigorous causal or theoretical link between magnitude/rank-based masking of W and the empirically observed structure of ΔW beyond correlation.

The theoretical contributions in Appendix B (Eckart-Young optimality, function-preservation at init, gradient mapping) are largely straightforward restatements of standard facts about SVD and LoRA-style reparameterization rather than novel theoretical insight specific to RLVR.

Some baseline comparisons are missing or under-motivated: DoRA, AdaLoRA, and VeRA are discussed in related work but not included in the empirical comparison; the specific SparseFT baseline is not clearly tied to a single well-defined prior method (multiple sparse FT papers are cited together).

Hyperparameters such as sparsity ratio ρ=0.2 and rank r=16 are fixed as defaults across most experiments without strong a priori justification, and although robustness curves are shown, the paper does not report how the optimal ρ or r was selected or whether it was tuned per baseline as well, raising some concern about fairness of comparison.

strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant question: whether SFT-oriented low-rank initialization strategies (PiSSA-style) are well suited to RLVR, and proposes a mechanism to reconcile the sparse/low-magnitude update patterns reported in RLVR literature with hardware-efficient dense low-rank computation.

Reasonably broad experimental scope: multiple backbones (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, plus smaller 1.5B/4B and larger 32B models in appendix), and multiple task domains (math, medical, coding), which is more coverage than many PEFT papers provide.

Includes ablations isolating the contribution of the initialization strategy (Random-r, Tail-r) and the two masking components (spectral vs Euclidean prior), which helps attribute gains to specific design choices rather than treating the method as a monolithic black box.

Some attempt at mechanistic grounding via spectral analysis (singular value decay of the masked subspace vs random/pretrained matrices) and subspace-alignment metrics (NSS, S_Head/S_Tail), which is a nice-to-have complement to pure benchmark numbers.

Practical efficiency reporting (params, VRAM, time/it) situates the method relative to full fine-tuning and unstructured sparse fine-tuning, addressing a real deployment concern the paper raises in its motivation.
weaknesses: All main results appear to be from a single random run ('based on a single random run', Appendix C.1), with no variance, standard deviation, or multiple-seed reporting anywhere in the paper. Given that RL training (GRPO) is well known to be high-variance, and that several ID benchmarks such as AIME24/AIME25 have only ~30 problems, the reported 1-2 point differences between GeoRA and baselines (e.g., 23.75 vs 22.50 vs 23.33 on AIME24 for Qwen3-8B) are within the noise floor of a single evaluation run and cannot be confidently attributed to the method rather than sampling variance. This substantially weakens the central empirical claim of 'consistent' superiority.

Full fine-tuning (FullFT) sometimes underperforms the proposed PEFT method and even plain LoRA on ID benchmarks (e.g., Qwen3-8B AIME24: FullFT 23.33 vs GeoRA 23.75; Llama AIME25: FullFT 8.25 vs GeoRA 8.75), which is atypical since FullFT should generally be an upper bound with sufficient tuning. This raises concern that the FullFT baseline (and possibly other baselines) may not be adequately tuned, undermining the validity of relative comparisons used to support GeoRA's claimed advantage.

The core mechanistic justification (Section 5.2, Figure 6a) risks being partly circular: WGeo is constructed by masking W to retain only small-magnitude/low-curvature entries, and then it is shown that WGeo's singular value spectrum resembles that of the pretrained weight rather than random noise. Given that masking preserves structured (non-random) entries of an already structured matrix, a heavy-tailed spectrum is unsurprising and does not strongly establish that this constructed subspace corresponds to the true 'effective RLVR update subspace' as opposed to an artifact of the masking procedure itself.

The theoretical appendix (B.1, B.2) restates well-known facts (Eckart-Young low-rank optimality, function-preserving initialization identical in spirit to PiSSA/OLoRA-style constructions) without offering a substantive new theoretical result specific to RLVR; framing this as formal justification somewhat overstates the technical contribution.

The method's construction (union of a spectral-prior mask and a Euclidean-prior mask, each defined via an arbitrary quantile threshold ρ, followed by a second SVD) is heuristic and only lightly justified; the ablation of ρ and rank is conducted on a single model (Qwen3-4B) and does not clarify how sensitive the method is across backbones or how ρ should be chosen in practice beyond the fixed value of 0.2 used throughout.

The efficiency comparison (Table 3) contrasts GeoRA's very small trainable parameter count against SparseFT's much larger reported parameter count without clarifying whether the two methods are matched under an equivalent effective sparsity/rank budget, making the apples-to-apples validity of the efficiency claim unclear.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the approach largely recombines existing observations from cited works (off-principal update directions, subnetwork sparsity in RL fine-tuning, spectral-prior initialization à la PiSSA/MiLoRA) into an engineering pipeline (magnitude/curvature masking + SVD-based init + frozen residual anchor), rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism or theoretical insight into RLVR-specific geometry.

strengths: Addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: existing SFT-oriented LoRA initialization (e.g., PiSSA) may be geometrically mismatched with RLVR's update dynamics, while sparse fine-tuning is hardware-inefficient; GeoRA is a reasonable attempt to reconcile both.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span model scales from 1.5B to 32B, two model families (Qwen, Llama), and three task domains (math, medical, coding), which supports the generality claim to some extent.
Useful ablations isolating the contribution of the geometry-aware initialization (vs. random-r and tail-r init) and of the two masking priors (spectral vs. Euclidean), showing both components matter.

Mechanism analysis (singular value spectra, Normalized Spectral Shift, subspace alignment) provides an interpretable narrative connecting the method to claimed properties of RLVR updates (low distortion of principal directions, adaptation concentrated in the tail subspace).
Efficiency analysis (Table 3) credibly shows the method avoids the hardware inefficiency of unstructured sparse fine-tuning while using far fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning.
Hyperparameter robustness studies (learning rate, rank, sparsity) suggest the method is less brittle than alternatives, which is practically valuable for RLVR where retraining is costly.
weaknesses: No variance/error bars or multiple seeds are reported anywhere; Appendix C.1 explicitly states results are from 'a single random run.' Given that RLVR training is known to be high-variance and benchmarks like AIME24/25 have only ~30 items, many of the reported gains (often 0.5-2 points) are within plausible seed noise, undermining the 'consistently outperforms' claim.

Effect sizes are inconsistent: GeoRA does not always beat the strongest baseline (e.g., on Llama-3.1-8B MATH500 and AIME25, FullFT/other baselines are better or comparable; on TruthfulQA, LoRA outperforms GeoRA). This weakens the claim of consistent superiority stated in the abstract and results sections.

The method's construction is somewhat circular/heuristic: the spectral prior masks entries based on a rank-r SVD approximation of W, and then a second SVD is performed on the resulting masked matrix WGeo to extract 'principal directions' for adapter initialization. The paper does not clearly justify why this double-SVD/mask pipeline specifically recovers the 'true' RLVR update subspace beyond post-hoc spectral similarity comparisons, which is weaker evidence than a first-principles derivation.

Secondary domain experiments (medical, coding) omit several baselines used in the main table (PiSSA, MiLoRA, SparseFT are missing from Tables 2), making the cross-domain generalization claim less rigorously supported than the math results.

The theoretical appendix (B) establishes only basic, largely definitional properties (Eckart-Young optimality of truncated SVD, function-preservation at initialization), which do not provide non-trivial guarantees specific to RLVR optimization dynamics; the core empirical claim about alignment with 'RLVR-preferred' subspaces rests entirely on the descriptive spectral analysis in Section 5, which is correlational rather than causal.

Main experiments fix rank r=16 and sparsity ratio ρ=0.2 without a systematic sweep showing this is a good default across all models/domains in the main comparison; the robustness sweep is only shown for one model (Qwen3-4B) and only under reward curves without downstream benchmark scores.

Reproducibility details for exact hyperparameters per experiment (e.g., whether other baselines like PiSSA/MiLoRA use identical LR schedules, warm-up, or per-method tuned LR) are not fully specified, raising some concern about fairness of comparison given GeoRA's own LR-robustness claims.
